title: ascii() on a truncated multibyte lead byte reads its continuation bytes past the end of the string. The 17.5 guard is Assert(*data > 0xC0), which is compiled out of a non-assert build
live_proof: CVE-2026-18024, fixed upstream in 849da8210539, which postdates the 17.5 pin
fidelity: real server, core, real allocator; reached by a C caller rather than by SQL. A text datum of one data byte, 0xF0. In a UTF8 database ascii() takes 0xF0 to promise three continuation bytes and reads data[1..3], three bytes past the end of a one-byte payload. The allocation is VARHDRSZ + 1 = 5 bytes, so whether an arm reports turns on whether its capability is narrowed to the 5 bytes palloc was asked for or to the aset chunk around them.

spatial.oracle: the three-byte over-read past a five-byte palloc chunk is reported, or the sequence completes and the arm did not see it

sublet.oracle: the three-byte over-read past a five-byte palloc chunk is reported, or the sequence completes and the arm did not see it

cheribsd-revocation.oracle: the three-byte over-read past a five-byte palloc chunk is reported, or the sequence completes and the arm did not see it

status: reachable on all three arms as of 2026-10-06 through the corpus module; no arm has run it yet
note: Reached by a C caller inside the backend, not by SQL. No SQL statement reaches this defect: it needs a multibyte database encoding and an invalid byte sequence stored at the same time, and those are mutually exclusive in PostgreSQL -- measured against a native 17.5 cluster on 2026-10-06, where a UTF8 database refused invalid bytes on every route, convert_from(bytea,'LATIN1') produced valid UTF-8, and a SQL_ASCII database had pg_encoding_max_length 1, which skips the branch. Upstream guards one of the two with Assert rather than a runtime check, which says the same thing. palloc does not validate, so the corpus module at ports/postgres/app/reach-module builds the datum and hands it to the defective code, which is how upstream's own note about already-corrupt on-disk data describes it being reached. What the arms then measure is the memory safety of the defective code once reached, not SQL-level exploitability. Reached and witnessed on the host cassert ASan build on 2026-10-06: TRAP: failed Assert("(data[i] & 0xC0) == 0x80"), src/backend/utils/adt/oracle_compat.c:965, with ascii+0x46b directly above corpus_ascii_truncated_lead in the stack. That assertion sits on the over-read itself. ASan alone does not report it, because the datum is a palloc chunk inside an aset block and ASan sees only the block -- which is the distinction this corpus exists to measure.
nested_why: The object is a palloc chunk, which AllocSet carves out of a block it took from malloc, so the defect is nested by the allocator that served it.
